@[[2fe61220-7bcd-41da-867c-fad95fc6e2b5]] You are the coordinator of this factory. Build the service described by the specification below,
coordinating the other seats to do it.

The specification, in full:
`/Users/ramymagdy/Developer/dark-factory-wearedevs/pocketful/spec/stage-1.md`

The repository the band commits to: `/Users/ramymagdy/Developer/band-work/result`

The work goes in `stage-1/` of that repository, and nowhere else in the filesystem. Build only
what this specification asks for. Requirements you can imagine, anticipate from experience, or
expect to be asked for later are out of scope: record them in your decisions log and leave them
there. A deliverable that reaches past the specification it was given is not a better
deliverable, and where deliverables are staged it destroys the evidence that they were built in
order.

`stage-1/` must be a complete, self-contained service: source, a `Dockerfile` that builds and
runs it with no other setup, and a `RUN.md` a stranger can follow. No submodules, no symlinks,
nothing it needs from outside the folder at run time, and no network access at run time.

The specification is the whole requirement. Any checks that arrive with it are a sample, not the
list, and satisfying the sample while missing the specification is a failure. The verifier
derives its own acceptance suite from the specification text as though no checks had been
supplied, and re-reads the specification for what those checks never asked about.

Every work item is accepted by the verifier and by no one else. Checking work yourself does not
make it verified, and an item with no verdict from the verifier is reported as unverified rather
than as done.

You have no one to ask. Resolve every ambiguity from the specification; where it is silent,
choose the reading most consistent with the rest of it, record the choice and why, and continue.
Do not stop to confirm anything with me and do not wait for a reply. If the band truly cannot
proceed, record the blocker, what you tried and the evidence you have, and report that as the
outcome.

Report when stage 1 is complete, or when you cannot go further: what was delivered, the
verifier's evidence for it, what is known to be weak or missing, and the decisions you made.

{"is_error":false,"name":"Bash","output":"# Pocketful — Stage 1: payments and settlements

This stage defines the initial service and its API.

Build from the supplied requirements. Source code, API documentation and schemas from
existing products in this domain must not be used.

## 1. Scope

Users can send money by handle, request money and split bills. Payments appear in an
activity feed with public or private visibility. Authorized operators can submit groups
of transfers as settlements. Only the HTTP API is required.

The following apply to all operations, including concurrent requests and retries:

1. The sum of wallet balances always equals the total seeded by the last `POST /_test/reset`.
2. No wallet balance may be negative, including transiently.
3. A payment request may move money at most once.

All amounts are exact integer counts of minor units. Deposits, top-ups, withdrawals,
cards and bank integrations are out of scope. Money moves only between existing wallets.

## 2. Delivery and deployment

Deliver an HTTP service, a `Dockerfile` and a `RUN.md` with a command that builds and
starts the service without manual setup. Language, framework and storage are unrestricted.
A `docker-compose.yml` is optional.

The submission is a containerized HTTP service, not a Python package. Python is not
required in the implementation. TypeScript/JavaScript, Go, Rust, Java, Python and any
other language are equally valid. The harness builds the submitted `Dockerfile`, starts
the resulting image and tests only its HTTP behavior; it does not import or execute the
submission's source files on the judge host.

The image must run on its own with `-e PORT=<port>` and a port mapping. Runtime networking
has no outbound access. All runtime dependencies, initialization and seed data must work
within that single container. Compose configuration is not used to start the service.

### Resource limits

The service must operate within these limits:

| Limit | Value |
|---|---|
| CPU | 2 vCPU |
| Memory | 2 GiB |

{"is_error":false,"name":"Bash","output":"# The factory

A three-seat band of coding agents that plans work, implements it, hands off evidence, and has
it independently checked before anything counts as done. It is task-agnostic: the seats' standing
instructions (`mandates/`) name no product, domain or interface. Everything specific to a job
goes in the task the human posts into the room.

## The crew

| Seat | Mandate | Runtime | Model | Owns |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| coordinator | [mandates/coordinator.md](mandates/coordinator.md) | Claude Code | claude-opus-5 | plan, sequencing, decisions log, acceptance bookkeeping, the report |
| implementer | [mandates/implementer.md](mandates/implementer.md) | Claude Code | claude-sonnet-5 | code and its tests, one work item at a time, handoffs with reproducible evidence |
| verifier | [mandates/verifier.md](mandates/verifier.md) | Claude Code | claude-opus-5 | acceptance checks derived from the specification before the build, independent reproduction, adversarial probes, the veto |

`seats.conf` is the single source of truth for these rows: it names each seat's runtime, model
and display name, `create-seats` launches from it, the mandates are tested against it, and the
mandates ship under the display names because that is what a reader matches them by.

**A roster of three different model families was measured first, and retired on arithmetic.**
One seat per family, chosen by handing each candidate a function with an off-by-one against a
stated rule and keeping the one that cited the line and named the breaking input. It built all
four stages of the practice track and passed every shipped check. It also cost $24.53 to do
that on a shared counter, which is a problem small enough to read in a minute. The graded work
is a different order of work, so the credit would not have reached the end of it. A run that
cannot afford to finish scores nothing, so the band went back to the runtime that is paid for.

Two seats now share a family, and that is a genuine loss: the veri…","tool_call_id":"toolu_01Y95JSzjHEmBCnu2oXDE2NK"}

WHAT TO BUILD
An executable acceptance suite that tests a running container over HTTP only. It must:
  - take a base URL from an environment variable (BASE_URL, default http://127.0.0.1:8080) so it can be pointed at any container on any port;
  - drive everything through POST /_test/reset fixtures, never through internal state;
  - exit non-zero on any failure and print, per failure: the spec reference, expected, actual, and the exact curl-equivalent to reproduce;
  - run in under a few minutes, and be runnable against a container started with --network none.
Ship a coverage map (stage-1/acceptance/COVERAGE.md) listing every requirement reference in the specification against the check(s) that cover it, and naming any requirement you deliberately left uncovered with the reason.

DERIVE IT FROM THE SPECIFICATION TEXT ALONE. The room plan's work-item acceptance criteria are the coordinator's floor, not your ceiling — they are a sample. Re-read the specification for what they never asked about. ### `POST /requests/{id}/decline`

Only the payer. No idempotency key. Returns `200` with the request, `status: "declined"`. Declining
an already-declined request is `200` with the current state — declining twice is not an error.
A `paid` or `cancelled` request is `409 request_not_pending`. Not the payer is `403 forbidden`.

### `POST /requests/{id}/cancel`

Only the requester. No idempotency key. Returns `200` with the request, `status: "cancelled"`.
Cancelling an already-cancelled request is `200`. A `paid` or `declined` request is
`409 request_not_pending`. Not the requester is `403 forbidden`.

### `GET /requests`

```http
GET /requests?direction=incoming&status=pending&limit=50&offset=0
```

Requests where the caller is the requester or the payer, and no others. Newest first by
`created_at`.

- `direction` is `incoming` (the caller is the payer), `outgoing` (the caller is the requester) or
  absent for both.
- `status` is one of the four statuses, or absent for all.
- `limit` defaults to 50, range 1 to 200. `offset` defaults to 0 and must be 0 or more. Outside
  either range is 422 `validation_failed`. An unknown `direction` or `status` value is also 422.
- `has_more` is true when items exist beyond the last one returned.

@[[0ca24821-4b32-4687-94b2-6129a6e91607]] Stage 1 standing brief (2/3) — decisions where the specification is silent, and the sequence.

These are resolved. Build to them. If you think one contradicts the specification text, quote the line and tell me before building it.
  D4  Every payment object carries settlement_id: null unless it is a settlement member. §11 says nonmembers expose null for that field, so the field exists on ordinary payments even though §8's example predates it.
  D5  Email equality for 409 email_taken is exact byte comparison. Case variants therefore collide at the derived handle and return 409 handle_taken. §4 lowercases only during handle derivation, so the email itself is not normalised.
  D6  Signup check order: field validation 422, then email_taken 409, then handle_taken 409.
  D7  email is valid when it contains exactly one '@' with a non-empty local part and a non-empty domain part. Nothing stricter — do not invent rules §6 does not state.
  D8  Timestamps are UTC with a literal +00:00 offset, never 'Z'. §3.4 wants an explicit offset and §8's own example is +00:00.
  D9  Ordering is newest-first by created_at, tie-broken by a monotonic creation sequence, newest sequence first. §8 excuses same-second ties only on /activity; GET /requests has no such excuse and needs a deterministic rule.
  D10 Seeded payments and requests get server timestamps assigned at reset in fixture-array order, so later in the array is newer. The fixture carries no timestamps but the list endpoints demand an order.
  D11 Do not enforce Content-Type on incoming requests; parse the body as JSON regardless. Rejecting on a missing request Content-Type would invent a 4xx §5 does not list.
  D12 An absent or empty request body is the JSON value {}. A present body that is not a JSON object ([1], "x", 3) is 400 malformed_request, per §7's 'after the body has parsed as a JSON object'.
  D13 For /requests/{id}/pay|decline|cancel, a known request with the wrong caller is 403 forbidden, not 404. §8 names 403 explicitly, and the specific rule beats §5's general 'not visible to this caller'.
  D14 Order on every idempotent write path: parse body (400) -> authenticate (401) -> key present and non-empty (400 missing_idempotency_key) -> key length 1..255 (422) -> key resolution (200 replay / 409 reuse) -> endpoint field validation (422/404/409). Key length goes ahead of resolution because an over-long key could never have been validly claimed.
  D15 On /settlements the operator check (403) runs immediately after authentication, before the idempotency key is examined, so a non-operator cannot claim keys in an operator's namespace.
  D16 The exported state is a full serialisation of the store: users with hashed passwords, tokens, balances, payments, requests, splits, settlements, operator ids, currency, the seeded total, the id and sequence counters, and every idempotency record with its original response body. Export the counters too — that is what stops the destination reissuing an id the source already used.
  D17 The verifier's acceptance suite lands at stage-1/acceptance/. Exclude it from the image with .dockerignore. The image must still build with that directory deleted.
  D18 No decisions file inside stage-1/. §2 asks for source, a Dockerfile and a RUN.md. The decisions log lives in the room plan.
  D19 No docker-compose.yml. §2 makes it optional and says compose is not used to start the service.

**What's in place:**
- **Room plan** (active snapshot) with a referenced inventory of every requirement in `spec/stage-1.md` — R1.1 through R11.19, each anchored to its section — eleven work items with command-checkable acceptance criteria, and a 19-entry decisions log with judgement calls marked.
- **Architecture** published as a standalone Arch JSON snapshot (edge → endpoints → domain → core state → packaging), embedded identically in the plan.
- **Shared board** loaded with A0 + W1–W11, each carrying its spec references and `Components:` node ids (typed component links aren't available on this Band version, so they're textual).

**Running in parallel right now:**
- **verifier** on A0 — acceptance suite derived from the specification alone, publishing to `stage-1/acceptance/` on `seat/verifier` with a coverage map. Told explicitly that the plan's criteria are a sample, and pointed at where they under-serve the spec. Probes withheld from the implementer.
- **implementer** on W1 — three-message standing brief (scope discipline, stack, binding constraints, all 19 decisions, sequence) plus W1's verbatim requirement text and eight acceptance criteria.

**Decisions worth surfacing:** Node 22 / zero deps / in-memory, chosen because a single-threaded event loop makes §1's "no transiently negative balance" and §7's "exactly one returns 201" structural rather than lock-dependent. Every payment object carries `settlement_id` (null for non-members) because §11 requires nonmembers to expose it. `GET /requests` same-second ties get a monotonic sequence tiebreak — §8 excuses ties only on `/activity`.

I won't check in again until stage 1 is frozen or the band is blocked. No item will be reported done without a verifier ACCEPT against the exact handed-off commit.

**Plan published** as the active room plan, with the architecture as a standalone Arch snapshot. It carries a referenced inventory of every requirement in `spec/stage-1.md` (R1.1–R11.19, each tied to its section), eleven work items with checkable acceptance criteria, and a decisions log of 19 entries — the judgement calls marked as such.

**Board loaded** with A0 + W1–W11: skeleton/packaging → reset+fixture → auth/handles/me → idempotency → payments → activity feed → requests → splits+rounding → export/import → settlements → hardening gate.

**Both seats are working now, in parallel:**
- verifier on A0 — deriving its acceptance suite from the specification text alone, publishing to `stage-1/acceptance/` on `seat/verifier` with a coverage map. It was told the plan's criteria are a sample, not the list, and pointed at the places they under-serve (§1 under load, §5 precedence when two errors collide, §7's R7.13, §9's share table, §10's preservation list, §11's entry-error ordering). Its adversarial probes stay unpublished so the implementer can't build to them.
- implementer on W1 — standing brief plus the full W1 requirement text and acceptance criteria.

**Stack decided:** Node.js 22, zero runtime dependencies, in-memory state. §2 leaves language free; built-in `crypto.scrypt` covers §6 hashing with nothing to install; a single-threaded event loop makes the §1 invariants true by construction rather than by locking; §10 says state needn't survive a restart. Three binding constraints ride with it — no `await` between claiming an idempotency key and committing, async scrypt confined to the two auth endpoints (with uniqueness re-checked after the await), and no 5xx ever.

Two things worth flagging now. §11 says nonmembers expose `null` for `settlement_id`, so **every** payment object carries that field even though §8's example predates it. And the specification is silent on same-second ordering for `GET /requests` while excusing it only for `/activity` — resolved with a monotonic creation-sequence tiebreak, recorded as a judgement call.

Scope is held to §1–§11. Deposits, directory/search, admin balance, password reset, refresh tokens, token expiry, persistence, rate limiting and compose are all recorded as out of scope and left there.

No item counts as done until the verifier posts ACCEPT for the exact handed-off commit. Anything without a verdict will be reported as unverified, not as done.

**The table-order argument doesn't hold.** The coordinator justified D22 partly as matching §8's split-table row order, and worried about an asymmetry with rejecting §11.7's sentence order. The §8 *payments* table lists `409 insufficient_funds` as its **first** row, above the 422 field rules — and nobody thinks `amount: 0` from an empty wallet is `insufficient_funds`. So row order isn't precedence anywhere in this spec, which means there's no asymmetry to defend and D22 should rest on coherence alone.

**D20's idempotency-key clause is unobservable.** I wrote a check for a 255-astral-code-point key, then found it can't be sent: HTTP header values carry octets, and a raw character above U+00FF is rejected before it leaves the client (`ERR_INVALID_CHAR`). UTF-8-encode instead and 255 emoji present as 1020 octets. For every key a client can transmit, code points, UTF-16 units and bytes coincide. I removed the check and documented why rather than pretending to test it. The handle-truncation clause is moot too — replacement runs first and yields pure ASCII. D20 is really a decision about the note, and only the note.

**A gap in D21, with a concrete case.** D21 fixes granularity but not its interaction with the order §4 already states. `İ` (U+0130) lowercases to *two* code points, so §4's lowercase-then-replace gives `İ@example.com` → `i_`, where replace-first gives `_`. Suite updated and pushed: ed8f273f133875da0fff22f14c2f542381a4a412 (short ed8f273), pasted from `git log -1 --format=%H`. 201 checks now, 16 of 16 decisions checked, **blocking floor unchanged at 159** — I added nothing to what can veto.

D20, D21, D22, D23 all accepted, all advisory, and I checked every currently-blocking check against them: **not one conflicts.** Every blocking precedence check I already had either agrees with D22/D23 or tests a case where they are silent. That is the part I most wanted to confirm before saying yes.

**Correction 1 — drop the table-order argument. It does not survive contact with §8.**
You justified D22 partly as "also §8's split-table order", and worried about an asymmetry with rejecting §11.7's sentence order for D23. There is no asymmetry to defend, because row order is not precedence anywhere in this specification. The §8 payments table reads, in order:

    | The caller's balance is below `amount`        | 409 insufficient_funds |
    | `amount` below 1, above 1000000000, ...      | 422 validation_failed  |

Funds is listed *first*, above field validation. No reading of D22 — or of anything — treats that as the highest precedence; a payment of `amount: 0` from an empty wallet is obviously not `insufficient_funds`. So the tables list codes, exactly as you read §11.7's sentence as listing codes. That makes D22 and D23 both free choices, consistently reasoned, and it removes the one argument someone could later use to attack D23 while citing D22. I would strike the "also §8's split-table order" clause from D22 and rest it on coherence alone, which is the stronger ground and the one you actually used.

**Correction 2 — D15's stated reason does not hold, though the decision is fine.**
D15's rationale is that checking the operator first "keeps a non-operator from claiming keys in an operator's namespace". There is no operator namespace: R7.3 scopes keys to the authenticated user, so a non-operator claiming a key only ever touches its own. The decision is still right and I am not asking you to change the behaviour — 403 before the key is clean and it stops a non-operator probing the endpoint, which is what your D22 chain says anyway. Only the reason in the log is wrong, and the log is the artefact that outlives us.

**D20's idempotency-key clause is not observable, and I removed my check for it.**
I wrote a check for a 255-astral-code-point key, then found it cannot be sent. An HTTP header value carries octets; a raw character above U+00FF is rejected before it leaves the client — Node throws `ERR_INVALID_CHAR`, and that is HTTP's rule, not Node's opinion. A client that UTF-8-encodes instead presents 1020 octets for 255 emoji, which is over 255 under every counting. So for every key a client can actually transmit, code points, UTF-16 units and bytes coincide, and the clause decides nothing. The note clause is where D20 genuinely bites, because a JSON string body carries astral characters fine. I have documented this in the suite rather than pretending to test it. The handle-truncation clause is similarly moot in a different way: replacement runs before truncation and produces pure ASCII, so by the time you truncate there is no difference between the units. **D20 is really a decision about the note, and only the note.**

**A gap in D21 worth pinning, with a concrete case.** D21 fixes the granularity but not the interaction with the order §4 already states. §4 says lowercase, *then* replace. Some lowercase mappings expand: U+0130 (`İ`) lowercases to two code points, `i` followed by U+0307 combining dot above. Follow §4's order and `İ@example.com` derives `i_` — the `i` survives and only the combining mark becomes an underscore. Replace before lowercasing and you get `_`. One code point in, a two-character handle out. This is settled by the specification text, not by D21, so it is a correctness question for the implementer rather than an interpretation for you; I have added it as a check with that noted. Worth restating when you assign W3, because it is the kind of thing that passes every ASCII test and fails one input.

**One clarification I would like, and one wording note on D22.**
- D22's last step bundles "state and funds 409". Those are two different 409s and they collide: a declined request whose payer also cannot afford it is both `request_not_pending` and `insufficient_funds`. I currently assert state first, on the grounds that §4 makes a terminal status final, and it is advisory. If you want that fixed, split the step.
- D22 puts "authorise 403" at step 3, ahead of "resource resolution 404" at step 6. For `/settlements` that is exactly D15 and it reads cleanly. For `/requests/{id}/*` it cannot be implemented literally — you cannot know the caller is not the payer without first finding the request. I take step 3 to mean endpoint-level authorisation and D13 to govern the resource-level 403, which is coherent and needs no change in behaviour. I also checked whether ordering the payer 403 against key resolution is observable, since R7.13 puts key resolution ahead of "current-resource checks": it is not. A key can only be claimed on a path where the caller's own attempt succeeded, and a non-payer's attempt never succeeds, so no caller can ever hold a claimed key on a path they are forbidden from. Either order is safe. Just worth the one-line wording fix so the implementer does not try to build step 3 literally.

**The verifier audited all four of my decisions and took down two of my reasons.** Both corrections were right, and I checked both against the spec text rather than accepting them on assertion:

- **D22's corroborating clause is struck.** I'd cited "§8's split-table order" as support. §8's payments table lists `insufficient_funds` *above* every 422 row (spec line 346) — so table order isn't merely uninformative about precedence, it encodes an order that's provably wrong, since `amount: 0` from an empty wallet isn't `insufficient_funds`. D22 now rests on coherence alone, which removes the only lever for attacking D23 while citing D22. That clause was reaching for corroboration I hadn't checked.
- **D15's reason was a fiction.** I'd justified checking operator status before the idempotency key as stopping a non-operator "claiming keys in an operator's namespace." No such namespace exists — R7.3 scopes keys to the authenticated user. Behaviour stands; the reason is replaced.

**Three substantive outcomes:**
- **D20 narrowed to the note alone.** The verifier tried to write a check for a 255-astral-code-point idempotency key and found it unsendable — HTTP header values carry octets, so code points, UTF-16 units and bytes coincide for any key a client can transmit. It documented the clause as untestable instead of writing a check that pretends.
- **C3 — a real defect caught before it exists.** §4 states lowercase *then* replace, and expanding lowercase mappings make that observable: I verified `İ@example.com` derives `i_`, not `_`, and `İstanbul@x.com` derives `i_stanbul`. Settled spec text, not interpretation. Goes into the W3 assignment verbatim.
- **D24 added, D22 reworded.** State 409 now explicitly precedes funds 409 (a terminal request can't move money whatever the balance). And D22's "authorise 403" is narrowed to *endpoint*-level — the verifier pointed out you can't know a caller isn't the payer without first finding the request, so the literal chain was unimplem…

**Correction 1 — accepted, and it is stronger than you put it.** §8's payments table, spec line 346, lists `insufficient_funds` *above* every 422 field row. So the table does not merely fail to encode precedence — it encodes an order that is provably wrong, since `amount: 0` from an empty wallet is plainly not `insufficient_funds`. The "also §8's split-table order" clause is struck from D22. It now rests on coherence alone, which as you say is the ground I actually used, and striking it removes the only lever for attacking D23 while citing D22. That clause was me reaching for corroboration I did not need and had not checked.

**Correction 2 — accepted.** There is no operator key namespace; R7.3 scopes keys to the authenticated user, so a non-operator claiming a key only ever touches its own. D15's behaviour stands unchanged; its stated reason is replaced with the honest one — it follows D22's chain and stops a non-operator probing the endpoint at all. You are right that the log is the artefact that outlives us, and a decision resting on a fiction is worse than no entry.

**D20 narrowed, as you found it.** An HTTP header value carries octets, a raw character above U+00FF never leaves the client, and UTF-8-encoding 255 emoji presents 1020 octets — over the limit under every counting. So for any key a client can transmit, code points, UTF-16 units and bytes coincide and the clause decides nothing. Truncation is moot for the separate reason that replacement yields pure ASCII first. **D20 is a decision about the note, and only the note.** Documenting an untestable clause as untestable instead of writing a check that pretends is the right call.

**Your D21 gap is a real defect waiting to happen, and it is not mine to interpret — §4 states the order.** Line 111: "take the local part, lowercase it, replace every character outside `[a-z0-9_]` with `_`, and truncate". I ran it: `İ` (U+0130) lowercases to `i` + U+0307, so `İ@example.com` derives `i_` and `İstanbul@x.com` derives `i_stanbul`. Replace-first gives `_` and `_stanbul`. Logged as C3 and it will be in the W3 assignment verbatim with those two cases, because you are right that it passes every ASCII test and fails one input.

**Your two requests, both granted:**
- **D22's last step is split. D24: state 409 before funds 409.** Your reading is confirmed as the decision. A terminal request cannot move money whatever the balance, so its status is dispositive without reference to any wallet, and R1.9 — "a payment request may move money at most once" — is a status rule, not a funds rule. A declined request whose payer is also short is `request_not_pending`.
- **D22 step 3 reworded to endpoint-level authorisation only**, with resource-level 403 sitting after resource resolution under D13. Your reading was the only implementable one and I should have written it that way. The full chain now reads: parse 400 → authenticate 401 → **endpoint** authorisation 403 → key (400 missing / 422 length / 200 replay / 409 reuse) → body field validation 422 → resource resolution 404 → **resource-level** authorisation 403 → state 409 → funds 409. Your proof that ordering the payer 403 against key resolution is unobservable — a key can only be claimed on a path where the caller's own attempt succeeded, and a non-payer's never succeeds — is what makes the rewording safe rather than merely tidier.

**On the settlements case where you lean the other way, I am holding D23, and I am recording your dissent in the log verbatim.** Your argument is good: nothing can leave a wallet that does not exist, and unlike §8's `self_payment` there is no caller handle known to exist. I am keeping 422 because one rule across all five write paths is cheaper to verify and to reason about than a rule with a single exception, and because the alternative makes resource resolution overtake an entry-internal check in exactly one place. That is a preference for coherence over your substantive point, not a refutation of it, and the log will say so with your reasoning attached rather than paraphrased. No money moves either way and it stays advisory. If a later stage gives the specification a reason to settle it, the dissent is where a reader should start.

Four decisions audited, none contradicting the specification, blocking floor unmoved at 159, and two of my reasons demolished — that is the audit doing exactly what it exists for. Content-Length: 0 rather than the GET-equivalent length, since Node
never writes HEAD body bytes and curl's `-X HEAD` (unlike `-I`) takes

will never arrive.

    settlements, operator ids, idempotency records, currency/minor_units,
    the seeded total, and the id/sequence counters (D16's exportable

    resume issuing ids without collision).
    
    Adds the fixture validator (src/lib/fixture.js): validates the whole
    fixture synchronously and throws 422 validation_failed on any
    problem before touching live state; only after every check passes
    does it hash seeded passwords via async scrypt in parallel
    (src/lib/password.js) and build the new state object. POST
    /_test/reset commits that candidate state in a single synchronous
    Store#replace, so a rejected reset can never partially mutate state
    and a concurrent reader never observes a half-built one.
    
    Seeded payments and requests get server timestamps and a shared
    monotonic sequence counter assigned in fixture-array order (D10);
    balances are taken as given, never replayed from seeded payments.
    
    C1 fix: sendJson/sendNoContent (src/lib/http.js) now set an explicit
    Content-Length on every response. A HEAD response declares
    Content-Length: 0 rather than the GET-equivalent length, since Node
    never writes HEAD body bytes and curl's `-X HEAD` (unlike `-I`) takes
    a nonzero Content-Length literally and hangs waiting for bytes that
    will never arrive.

D25 (2026-09-29): **No per-route request timeout is ever to be built**, in W11 or anywhere. §2's

under load ("must operate within these limits"), not a feature to implement — nothing in §2 asks for
enforcement, and a self-imposed timeout would have to either truncate a response or return 5xx, both
forbidden by §5. Staying inside the budget is proved only by measurement under load at W11 (the
mixed 50-in-flight test), never by timeout code.

confirmed the reading was correct and recorded it as a decision so it isn't relitigated in later items
(W7+ concurrency work, W11 hardening).

**How to apply:** don't add `setTimeout`/`req.setTimeout`/route-level deadlines when building any

I checked at source: `src/lib/password.js` is untouched between 116b97d and cfc7be43. The scrypt cost parameter is still Node's default. What you changed is how MANY hashes are computed, not what each one costs.

R6.11 names scrypt and sets no cost floor, so lowering the work factor satisfies it. Keep the memoisation as well; the two are complementary, not alternatives.

  7. D28: any script you cite in an Evidence line lives in `stage-1/tests/`, committed, and `.dockerignore`d like `acceptance/`.
  8. No regression on suites 01, 02 and 03.

    Acceptance suite: a signup must not mint a seeded user id
    
    The blocking check that matters most so far. The specification's own signup
    example returns "user_id": "u_1" and its fixture example seeds ids of that shape,
    so a fixture seeding u_1 is ordinary input. A counter-based generator that
    restarts at 1 after each reset mints u_1 again, the seeded account is displaced in
    the id map, and the seeded user's own bearer [redacted] begins resolving to the account
    that displaced it. The check asserts the decisive property directly: after four
    signups, the seeded user's token still identifies the seeded user, with the same
    handle and the same balance.
    
    Also adds an advisory companion to the reset-budget check that removes the one
    regularity the blocking version relies on -- every seeded user sharing a password.
    Memoising by password value fixes the common case completely; the residual
    per-distinct-password cost stays visible rather than being hidden by a fixture
    shape that happens to suit the memoisation.

  1. BLOCKING — a signup can mint a user id the fixture already seeded, and the seeded
     user's bearer token then authenticates as the account that displaced it.
     Reference: R4.3, R1.7, R6.10; §6's own signup example returns "user_id": "u_1".
     Expected: a seeded account's token keeps identifying that account.
     Actual:   `store.nextId` restarts its counter at 1 on every reset and has no guard
               against an id already present in the seeded state. `usersById.set(id, user)`
               then overwrites the seeded entry, while `usersByHandle` still holds the old
               object — the state is internally inconsistent from that moment.
               Measured, three times, seeding u_1, u_2 and u_3 in turn:

                 reset with users:[{id:"u_1", handle:"seeded", balance:10000}]
                 login seeded@example.com                  -> token T
                 GET /me  (T)  -> {"user_id":"u_1","handle":"seeded","balance":10000}
                 POST /auth/signup intruder@example.com    -> {"user_id":"u_1", ...}
                 GET /me  (T)  -> {"user_id":"u_1","handle":"intruder","balance":0}

               10000 is orphaned in the handle map, so the sum over wallets no longer equals
               the seeded total either. Handle uniqueness *is* checked, so a signup cannot
               steal a handle — only an id, which is what tokens resolve through.

'The key is scoped to the authenticated user. Two different users may use the same key string with no interaction between them.'
'A replay means the same user sending the same method, the same path and the same body. The same key with the same body on a different path is a different request, not a replay, and must succeed normally.'
Table — Header absent or empty: 400 missing_idempotency_key. First use of the key: the normal response, 201. Replay (same key, same body): 200, body identical to the original response as a JSON value. Same key, different body: 409 idempotency_key_reuse. Key reused after the original request failed with 4xx: treated as a first use.
'"Same body" means the same JSON value after parsing — key order and whitespace do not matter.'
'For concurrent identical requests with an unused key, exactly one returns 201. The others return 200 with the same body. The operation takes effect only once.'
'A successful replay returns the original response, even after the resource changes or is cancelled. It makes no further state changes.'
'After the body has parsed as a JSON object and the caller is authenticated, an already claimed key is resolved before endpoint field validation or current-resource checks. Thus changing a successful request to an invalid body with the same key still returns 409 idempotency_key_reuse.'

|---|---|

The debit and the credit are one atomic step. A payment is never visible in one wallet and not the
other, and a failed payment leaves no trace in either.

`note` is stored and returned verbatim: no trimming, no escaping, no normalisation. Unicode and
emoji survive a round trip byte for byte.

**A request may exceed the payer's balance.** That is a legal state, not an error at creation time:
the request stays `pending` until it is paid, declined or cancelled, and an attempt to pay it while

**Visibility belongs to the payment, not the request.** The payer chooses it when the money moves.
A request carries no visibility of its own and never appears in anyone else's feed.

### The feed contract

`GET /activity` returns payments only. A payment appears for a caller **if and only if** its
`visibility` is `public`, **or** the caller is its sender or its receiver. There is no other rule,
no follow graph and no mute list. Requests never appear in the activity feed; they are read through
`GET /requests`, which returns only requests where the caller is the requester or the payer.

A split is not a feed item. The requests it creates are visible to their own two parties, and the
payments that eventually fulfil them follow the rule above.

Visibility is **one value on the payment**, seen identically by both parties and by everyone else.
A `private` payment is hidden from third parties, not from its own receiver.

### Arithmetic range

`amount` is at most `1000000000` on any single request, and no operation produces a balance outside
±2⁵³. Monetary arithmetic must preserve exact minor-unit values without rounding error.

**Goal.** One gate serving all five write paths.
**Refs.** R7.1–R7.13, R5.3, R5.13, R5.7. Plus D14 and D22's key steps.
**Accept.**
1. Missing or empty key → 400 `missing_idempotency_key`.
2. A 256-character key → 422; 255 and 1 accepted.
3. First use → 201; identical replay → 200, same JSON value, no second movement.
4. Same key, different body → 409 `idempotency_key_reuse`.
5. Same key, same body, **different path** → succeeds normally.
6. Same key string from a different user → succeeds normally.
7. A key whose first use returned 4xx is reusable and then returns 201.
8. A successful key replayed with an invalid body → 409, not 422 (R7.13).
9. 20 concurrent identical requests with one unused key → exactly one 201, nineteen 200s, one movement.
**Deps.** W3.

### W5 — Payments
**Refs.** R8.2–R8.11, R1.8, R1.10, R4.2, R4.9, R4.17, R5.10. Plus D4, D20, D22.

1. Valid payment → 201 with every field of R8.3, `request_id: null`, `settlement_id: null`, RFC 3339 `created_at` with an explicit offset; both balances move by exactly `amount`.
2. Insufficient funds → 409 and **no** balance change on either side.
3. `amount` of `0`, `-1`, `1000000001`, `1.5`, `"100"`, `true`, `null` → 422; `1000.0` and `1e3` succeed as 1000.
4. `to_handle` equal to the caller's handle → 422 `self_payment`.
5. **D20:** a note of 200 code points succeeds and 201 → 422, counted in code points — so 200 astral emoji is a valid note. `note: null` and `note: 5` → 422; omitted defaults to `""`.
6. `visibility` omitted defaults to `"public"`; `"secret"` → 422.
7. Unknown `to_handle` → 404.
8. **D22:** invalid `amount` together with an unknown `to_handle` → 422, not 404.
9. A note of emoji and combining marks round-trips byte for byte through the response and `GET /activity`.
10. 50 concurrent payments across a ring of wallets: total conserved, never negative, no 5xx.
**Deps.** W4.

## `VERDICT W2 @ 784ea09aea6bc5f019d4021e0d23e18080aea789: ACCEPT`

**Findings:**
1. *(withdrawn — my error, not the implementer's)* I first read criterion 5's "balance outside ±2⁵³" as failing, on `balance: 9007199254740993`. That literal parses to `9007199254740992` = 2⁵³ exactly, which is **not** outside the range, so 204 is right. Re-probed the real boundary: `9007199254740992` → 204, `9007199254740994` → 422 `validation_failed` "exceeds the safe range", `-9007199254740994` → 422, `1e17` → 422, `1e400` → 422 "must be an integral number". RFC 9110 §9.3.2 requires a general-purpose server to support HEAD wherever it supports GET, and an orchestrator health probe using HEAD would read this as unhealthy. Advisory, exactly as C1 was: the specification never names HEAD, so blocking would be me legislating. Reproduce: `curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}' -I http://127.0.0.1:18082/health` → `404`.

## Fix 1 — W2b finding 1. BLOCKING. R6.11.

**The defect, in full.** `src/lib/fixture.js` hashes once per distinct password value —
`hashByPassword.set(password, await hashPassword(password))` — and assigns that one string to every
user holding that password. Four users sharing a password get four byte-identical `password_hash`
strings: same salt, same digest. The verifier measured 6 users over 2 password values → **2 distinct
hashes, group sizes [4, 2]**.

**Why it is blocking rather than cosmetic.** `GET /_test/export` is unauthenticated (R10.1) and emits
`password_hash` verbatim, so any caller can partition the seeded user table into password-equality
classes, and one successful dictionary attack recovers a whole class for the cost of one. R6.11 names
bcrypt, scrypt and Argon2; per-record salting is not an embellishment of those functions, it is the
property they exist to provide and the standard "or an equivalent" is measured against. R6.11 is
W2b's own reference via D26b.

**Expected:** one salt per stored record, so stored hashes carry no information about which passwords
are equal.

with the headroom it already has. `hashPassword` already generates a fresh salt per call, so this is
a deletion in `fixture.js` and **no change to `password.js`**.

Routing note while you build W5 — the verifier's suite head moved again and you do not have it. You
merged `d861920` at `2b12cd0`; the head is now **`74e8ee4`**. Merge it before you run your gate.

**What it adds: two checks for W5 criterion 11**, written before your build, both currently **failing**
at `5a9cffd` on the absent `/payments` route by design. They are the checks behind the clause I added
to criterion 11, and the gap they close was real — suite `05` has eighteen idempotency checks and none
of them asserted a record reaches `GET /_test/export`, while suite `10`'s export work is the W9 round
trip. So harness-reachable versus reachable-through-the-shipped-service had no check behind it at all.

1. **A completed idempotent request reaches the export through the delivered image** — the record
   carries its request body, its original response verbatim, its original status, and its
   `(user, method, path)` scope. R10.11 names body and response specifically because R10.13 and R10.14
   depend on both: a retry after import has to return what the first call returned, and a record that
   lost either is one W9 cannot restore a retry from.
2. **A key freed by a 4xx contributes no record**, or R10.13's "failed request keys remain reusable"
   breaks on the destination.

**Read them, do not change them** — same rule as before. If your W5 work moves or reshapes anything
they import, say so in the handoff and the verifier will re-derive rather than treat a load failure as
a finding.

first run and passed for the *wrong reason*: the payment 4xx'd because `/payments` does not exist yet,

that goes green before the feature exists is worth less than no check, since it will be green at W5 as
well and nobody will look at it again. If any test you write for W5 passes before the route is
registered, that is a finding about the test.

`src/lib/auth.js` and the id-minting path, D45 on any timing number.

**W5 REJECTED at `3349702` on C6, one blocking finding, and it is not in `payments.js`.** One of three
rejections used. Everything else in the endpoint reproduced clean — details at the end, because they
matter and none of them need changing.

**Before the fix: merge `seat/verifier` at `f476e02`.** Two C6 checks, plus a D47 audit of the
verifier's own 213 checks that changed the headline counts. Its run reads `92 / 103 / 18` where yours
read `99 / 96 / 16`; that is **the suite changing, not W5 regressing.** Seven of the delta are honest
failures where vacuous passes used to be, two are C6's new checks.

---

## The finding, in full. C6 confirmed, and worse than my repro predicted.

I raised this as a bound being unenforced. I also wrote that R1.7 would survive because "the money was
conserved, it is the bound that broke." **That was wrong, and the way it is wrong is the whole
finding.** Above 2⁵³ the integer grid is no longer unit-spaced, so a credit of 1 rounds away while the
matching debit lands exactly:

```
reset: two users each seeded 9007199254740992   -> 204 (each individually legal, total 2^54)
50x POST /payments {to_handle, amount: 1}       -> 50x 201, each reporting amount 1
sender   9007199254740992 -> 9007199254740942   (debited 50)
receiver 9007199254740992 -> 9007199254740992   (credited 0)
sum 18014398509481934 vs seeded_total 18014398509481984
```

**Fifty minor units destroyed.** Not moved, not mislaid — gone, through fifty requests the service
answered `201` and reported as `amount: 1`. R1.7 is §1.1, the first invariant in the document, and §4
requires monetary arithmetic to "preserve exact minor-unit values **without rounding error**". This is
that rounding error.

A single payment hides it completely: one credit of 1 leaves the sum unchanged because the sum itself
rounds at that magnitude. It takes a run before the loss is arithmetically visible, which is why no
criterion-level check would have caught it.

The bound also breaks separately, in the other direction, with money conserved:
```
reset: src 1000000000, dst 9007199254740992     -> 204
POST /payments {to_handle: dst, amount: 1000000000} -> 201
dst balance 9007200254740992 = 2^53 + 1000000000
```

**Advisory from the verdict, and it is the reason this needed a check rather than a note:** `GET /me`
and the export both report the rounded balance consistently, so nothing disagrees with anything. The
loss is invisible from inside the API.

**Scope, by D40:** R4.17 is in W5's reference set and not W2's, and the violating operation is
`POST /payments`. So it is W5's finding even though the remedy lands in `fixture.js`. W2's ACCEPT at
`5a9cffd` stands — no payment path existed there, so R1.7 held. Same reasoning that kept the salt
finding off W2.

---

## The fix — D49. The outcome is the requirement; the mechanism is yours.

**Refuse at reset any fixture whose seeded balances sum above 2⁵³**, 422 `validation_failed`.

Both halves of C6 then die at once, by construction rather than by a check at every operation:
balances are non-negative (§1.2) and R1.7 conserves the seeded total, so a total at or below 2⁵³
bounds every balance forever — through payments now, and splits and settlements later — and every
intermediate sum stays on the unit-spaced part of the integer grid, where §4's "without rounding
error" is achievable at all. 422 at reset invents nothing: §4 already answers 422 for a fixture whose
individual balance is out of range, and this is the same class of error one level up. Rejecting the
payment instead would need a payment-time code §8's table does not list, and would leave the
arithmetic hazard live for every other write path.

**The verifier measured this before I ordered it** rather than taking my word: seeded total
`9007199254740942`, fifty payments of 1, R1.7 held exactly. It states both new checks pass if the
fixture is refused at reset **and** pass if balances stay exact some other way — so if you see a
better mechanism, take it. It is asserting the outcome.

`fixture.js` is in scope for this commit. D39's reset-fixture clause is spent; `src/lib/auth.js` and
the id-minting path stay off limits.

**Acceptance.** `--only "destroys money or exceeds the arithmetic range"` and
`--only "single large payment cannot push"` both pass. W5's twelve criteria stay green. Groups `01`–`05`
no worse than the verifier's `f476e02` baseline, named per D33.

---

## What was verified and is right, so you know what not to touch

C6 is the only thing wrong with this endpoint. The verifier reproduced, beyond the criteria: 60
simultaneous 200-unit payments from a 10000 balance → exactly 50 created, 10 `insufficient_funds`,
sender drained to exactly 0, R1.7 exact, nothing negative. Payments crossing both ways between the
same two wallets → conserved. 25 racers on one key → one 201, twenty-four 200s, byte-identical bodies,
money moved once. D22's chain end to end including the two orderings easy to get backwards — an invalid
amount *with* an unknown handle is 422 not 404, and `self_payment` beats `insufficient_funds` on a zero
balance while an invalid amount beats `self_payment`. All seven documented §8 errors with exact status,
code and a non-empty message. Twelve hostile bodies — 400-deep nesting, a 500 KB field, `1e309`, `-0`,
duplicate JSON keys, a lone surrogate — no 5xx, every 4xx enveloped, service healthy after.

**On the 404 paths you hardened under D47, the verifier settled why your control was necessary rather
than belt-and-braces:** the two 404s share a status *and* a code, differing only in message, which §5
does not make contractual. So a check asserting status+code genuinely cannot distinguish "unknown
handle" from "absent route". Your control payment is the only thing that can.

**D43 carry-forward at this commit:** W1, W2, W2b and W3 all carry. **W4 carries and is now stronger** —
its gate had only ever run against a harness; at this commit the verifier exercised it through the
delivered image on a real write path and criteria 1–11 hold there. That is criterion 11's
delivered-image clause paying for itself.

**D48 applied and not a basis for rejection:** criterion 9 is the response round-trip only at W5, and
the verifier confirmed it — quotes, backslash, `\u0000`, ZWJ, RTL and combining marks all byte-identical
in the 201 and unchanged into the export. Your `Unverified:` note was correct.

**Next:** the D49 fix as its own commit, handed to the verifier, CC me with the body in the CC.

## W6 — Activity feed and shared pagination. Build on `65f4208`.

**Refs.** R4.13, R4.15, R4.16, R8.35–R8.37, R5.11, R5.14, R5.15. Plus D9, D30 and the §8 `/requests`
pagination paragraph that R8.37 imports.

**Criteria.**
1. A `public` payment between A and B is visible to A, B and an unrelated C.
2. A `private` payment between A and B is visible to A and B and **absent** for C.
3. **Relaxed — read this one carefully, it is looser than you may expect.** Newest first by
   `created_at`. A tie within the same second is **not** required to follow any particular order:
   R8.36 excuses exactly that on `/activity`. But with no concurrent writes, two identical calls must
   return the same order, because criterion 4's walk depends on it. **Do not** build a tie-break to
   satisfy this criterion — if one falls out of your existing sequence, fine; if it does not, that is
   not a defect here. (D51. `GET /requests` at W7 is different: R8.36 gives it no such excuse, so D9's
   deterministic tie-break is required there.)
4. `limit=1&offset=0` then `offset=1` walk the list; `has_more` true exactly while items remain.
5. `limit=0`, `limit=201`, `limit=-1`, `offset=-1` → 422; `limit=1e9`, `limit=4.0`, `limit=+4` → 422
   (R5.11 — an integer query parameter is plain decimal digits, whatever the numeric value).
6. Unknown query parameters ignored.
7. No token → 401.
8. **Carried from W5 criterion 9 by D48:** a note of emoji and combining marks round-trips byte for
   byte through `GET /activity`, not only through the payment response.
9. The envelope is exactly `{"payments": [...], "has_more": bool}` (R8.35), and each item carries every
   field of R8.3 — identical to what `POST /payments` returned for that payment.
10. Absent `limit` defaults to **50** and absent `offset` to **0** (§8's `/requests` paragraph,
    imported here by R8.37). Observable with 51 visible payments: 50 returned, `has_more` true.
11. A seeded **request** never appears in `/activity` — R4.13 is "payments only", and §4's own fixture
    seeds `rq_1`, so this is checkable at this item rather than at W7.
12. **R4.16:** one visibility value seen identically. A `public` payment's object is byte-identical as
    read by its sender, its receiver and an unrelated caller.
13. **D30:** if this item adds a key to `emptyState()`, `serializeState()` is extended in the same
    commit, and the export-coverage guard still passes.

Criteria 9–13 are additions and all five are in the plan (rev 20) as of this message, per D38.

**Not in this item — R4.15.** "A split is not a feed item" is in W6's reference set, but nothing can
create a split until W8, so the check is **carried to W8** (D52). Do not build toward it here. Useful

**The review range rule, since a merge will sit between this handoff and the last:** state
`git diff --stat $(git rev-parse HEAD^)..HEAD`, not the range from the previous handoff. That is the
one thing to fix from W5's paperwork.

## What landed at W5, briefly, because two parts of it are worth carrying forward

**Your BigInt choice was load-bearing, not decorative, and the verifier proved it.** Balances of
`9007199254740991` and `2` sum to 2⁵³+1 in exact arithmetic but to **exactly 2⁵³** in floats — so a
`seededTotal`-based check would have accepted the very fixture the rule exists to refuse. Rejected by
yours. Same for twenty balances summing to 2⁵³+9 where float accumulation loses the excess. It also
checked that `BigInt()` throwing on non-integers had not turned fixture errors into generic 400s:
non-integral, string, `null`, `true`, `1e999`, negative, over-cap and missing `balance` all still
return 422, because your integer validation runs first.

**The verifier's own check on your fix was vacuous and it said so.** `single large payment cannot push`
carried `if (res.status === 422) return;` — harmless while the oversize fixture was still accepted,
vacuous the moment your fix made refusal the live path. It was caught by the guard the verifier had
landed ten minutes earlier, which fired for the first time on its own author's check. So your evidence
line `--only "single large payment cannot push" -> ok` was **true and meant nothing** until `d39d965`.
That is now D50, and it applies to your tests as much as to the suite.

D51 is a warning about a class, not just about one criterion, so I ran it back over my own `/activity` checks before W6 is built rather than after it fails one. **Result: clean, and here is what "clean" rests on**, since a negative audit is only worth anything if you can see what was examined.

- **The blocking ordering check is exactly R8.35 and no stricter.** `the feed is ordered newest first` uses `nonIncreasing(payments, 'created_at')`, which returns false only when `prev < next` — **equal timestamps pass**. Six payments created in a burst share a second and the check does not care how they are ordered among themselves. That is R8.36's exemption honoured, not accidentally survived.
- **The one check that does demand fixture-array order on `/activity` is advisory**, and cites D10 rather than a spec reference. That is the right severity for something R8.36 exempts: the decision is recorded and visible, and it cannot veto.
- **The pagination check does every write before it pages**, then pages a static feed, and asserts only page sizes, `has_more`, the default limit and the 422s. It never asserts which item lands on which page. So it demands determinism under a static state — which is what survives D51 — and never stability under concurrent writes, which R8.36 excuses.

`stage-1/acceptance/COVERAGE.md` has claimed since A0 that R8.36 is "an explicit relaxation, not a requirement — the suite relies on it: it never asserts an order between two items created in the same second, and never asserts pagination stability during concurrent writes." That was a claim about my own code that nobody had checked. It is now checked, and it holds.

**D52 matches where my checks already sit**, which is worth confirming rather than assuming: the two split-specific R4.15 checks are in group `08`, not `07`. Nothing in my suite tries to assert "a split is not a feed item" before splits exist.

**One thing to name in advance so it is not re-litigated at the W6 handoff.** Group `07` has a check tagged R4.15 — `payments settling a request appear in the feed under the ordinary rule` — which needs `POST /requests/{id}/pay`. That is **W7**, not W6 and not W8. It will be an out-of-scope-at-this-commit failure in group 07 when W6 lands, and it is neither a W6 defect nor a D52 placement error: R4.15 has two halves, and the half about payments that settle requests belongs to the item that provides the settling path.

**Refs.** R1.9, R4.10–R4.12, R4.14, R8.12–R8.27. Plus C2, D9, D13, D20, D22, D24.

**Criteria.**
1. Create → 201 with R8.13's shape, `status: "pending"`, `payment_id: null`.
2. A request above the payer's balance is created normally (R8.15); paying it → 409 `insufficient_funds`, no state change; after the payer receives money the same request pays.
3. Pay → 201 with a payment whose `request_id` is this request; the request becomes `paid` and carries the new `payment_id`; money moved exactly once.
4. Paying a terminal request with a **new** key → 409 `request_not_pending`; replaying the **original successful** pay → 200 with the original payment body, no further movement, **and not 409** even though the request is already `paid` (§8 states this explicitly).
5. `{}` and `{"visibility":"public"}` under the same key → 409 `idempotency_key_reuse` (R8.16) — they are different JSON values.
6. Non-payer pay → 403; non-payer decline → 403; non-requester cancel → 403; unknown id → 404.
7. Decline twice → 200 both times; cancel twice → 200 both times; decline a cancelled request → 409.
8. **D24:** a terminal request whose payer is also short → `request_not_pending`, not `insufficient_funds`. Includes the sharp case: a payer who spends its last funds paying the request, then retries under a fresh key against an empty wallet.
9. **C2:** `POST /requests/%ZZ/pay` → 404 `not_found`, not 400. `decodeURIComponent` on a captured path parameter must not throw into the generic handler.
10. `GET /requests` returns only requests where the caller is requester or payer; a third party sees none.
11. `direction`/`status` filter correctly; `direction=sideways` and `status=weird` → 422.
12. Newest first by `created_at`, **ties broken deterministically by creation sequence — required here, unlike `/activity`.** R8.36 exempts the feed and gives `GET /requests` no such exemption (D9, D51). 14. 20 simultaneous pays of one request with distinct keys → exactly one 201, the rest 409, money moved once (R1.9).
15. **R4.15's second half, placed here by D52 as amended:** a payment that settles a request appears in `GET /activity` under the ordinary feed rule — visible to its two parties, and to a third party iff its `visibility` is `public`. Correction to my W7 assignment (9eebc988), time-sensitive because you are building now. **Two things
change; neither adds work.**

**1. Merge `seat/verifier` at `a61dd49`, not `31a1474`.** My pointer was one commit stale — we crossed.
The head is 215 checks, not 213, and the two added ones land on **your** endpoint:
`paging a static request list composes into the unpaged list exactly once` (R8.25, R8.26) and its
`/activity` twin. The `/requests` one is **blocking**. If you build against 213 you meet it for the
first time at the handoff, which is the wrong time.

**What it requires, and why it is nothing new:** every write happens first, then the unpaged read must
be stable across two calls, then a walk four at a time must compose into the unpaged list exactly once
in the same order, with `has_more` correct at every offset. W6's `lib/pagination.js` over a stable sort
of an unchanged array already satisfies the `/activity` half unmodified — the `/requests` half fails
today only because the endpoint does not exist. Reuse the same shape.

What it rules out is a `/requests` implementation whose order varies between calls on an unchanged
state, which would be invisible to every other check in the suite and would make pagination silently
lossy — a list returning one item on two pages, or skipping one mid-list.

**It does not ask for D9's tie-break.** Two same-second requests may come back in either order; the
check only requires the order be the *same* across a paged walk and a repeated read.

**2. Criterion 12's tie-break and the suite's tie-break check are two different instruments, and at the
W7 verdict they will carry different severities.** Now D57 in the plan, so it is settled before it can
be argued:

- **Composition and stability** — spec-level, §8's paging contract. The verifier blocks.
- **The particular tie *order*** — rests on D9, which is my decision, not specification text. The
  verifier's own check stays **advisory**, correctly; its veto rests on the document.
- **Criterion 12 itself** — the verifier has said it will verify it as **binding** at W7 because I made
  it a criterion.

So a same-second ordering failure would be blocking as a criterion and advisory in the suite. That is
not a contradiction: the verifier owns whether the service violates the specification, I own whether the
item matches the plan, and an item needs both. Practically this is probably moot — your sequence
tie-break already exists and serves both endpoints — which is exactly why it is worth writing down now.

Everything else in the assignment stands: criteria 1–18, D39, D33, D45, D47, D50, and the review range
as `git diff --stat $(git rev-parse HEAD^)..HEAD`.

An implementer building against 213 meets that check for the first time at the handoff, which is the wrong time to meet it. I have told it to merge `a61dd49`, and that the requirement is satisfied by W6's `lib/pagination.js` over a stable sort — nothing new to build.

**D56 records what you did and, more importantly, how you found it.** Running D51 in the mirror direction is the move I would not have thought to ask for: D51 asks whether a check is stricter than the specification, and the opposite failure — too weak where the rule is strict — has no symptom at all. Group `07` with zero composition assertions and group `06` with one covering the first page would have passed a list returning an item on two pages or skipping one mid-list.

The detection mechanism is the part I have written into the entry rather than the finding: **your own W6 probe covered what the permanent checks did not, and the probe passed.** So nothing was wrong with the service, nothing failed, and nobody would ever have looked. A failing probe announces itself; a passing probe that reaches further than the suite is silent — and the suite is what survives to the freeze while a probe is one seat's scratch work. That is the same family as D50 and D53: a green that means less than it appears to. The rule is now that probe coverage gets reconciled against the permanent checks and what only a probe covers gets promoted.

The proxy demonstration is the right standard too — a repeated item, a skipped item and an unstable unpaged order all caught, passthrough passing. D47 asks for a check shown failing for the intended reason, and three distinct wrong behaviours plus a control is more than that asks for.

**Your resolution of the severity split is better than the one I had drafted, and I have adopted it verbatim into D57.** I was going to say the criterion binds me regardless of your severity; you have put it more cleanly — your own check stays advisory on its own grounds, and you verify *the criterion* as binding because I made it one. Nothing has to change its grounds: the verifier owns whether the service violates the document, I own whether the item matches the plan, and an item needs both. A same-second ordering failure being blocking as a criterion and advisory in the suite is a coherent record, not a contradiction, and it is on paper before it can be argued.

The one thing I have added on my side: **an ACCEPT is necessary for an item to be done, not sufficient.** I do not close an item whose criteria are unmet, and I do not ask you to raise a severity your own reasoning does not support. Those are the two failure modes that would make the split incoherent, and they are both mine to avoid.

**On D54** — agreed that the diagnosis is what makes it usable, and naming the dependency in a check's own text when its last step reaches past its group is a better fix than leaving it for the next audit. Three instances traced is where I would have stopped counting; that you will annotate forward is what stops there being a fourth.

D56 applied to my own instruments. I ran it across all nine areas my probes touch; two were genuinely suite-invisible and got promoted.

never makes key order contractual. That stands. The verifier then refined it at the verdict and the

right**, because R7.7 requires the *original response body verbatim*. The distinction is whether one
response is reproducing itself or two responses are being compared. Two call sites agreeing field-wise

## D60 — the export contract grew, and it is worth recording as a contract rather than a diff

The split mapper references its requests **by id** (`request_ids`), not by embedding them. The
implementer's reason is sound and I have preserved it: requests already have their own top-level export
entry, and a copy embedded in the split would be frozen at split-creation time and drift from the live
status a later payment produces — so the embedded copy would contradict the top-level one and an import
would have to choose. Referencing by id leaves one authority for a request's state.

D31 said the export shape was the implementer's design and would grow freely. This is it growing, and
the consequence for W9 is concrete: **import must resolve ids rather than read a self-contained split
record.** That is now W9 criterion 14 — a split exported with `request_ids` must, after import into B,
resolve to requests that exist with the same ids and the live status they had on A. Not a frozen copy,
not a dangling id.

Worth noting the create *response* still embeds full live request objects via `serializeRequest`. The
API shape §8 documents and the export shape are different things and keeping them different is right —
criterion 13 is about the response, criterion 15 about the export.

## C8 — raised by me, closed by me, directed into W9. No action at W8.

**The D30 guard derives from `emptyState()`'s top-level keys, so a mapper that drops a field *inside* a
record passes it.** W8 is the commit where that stops being hypothetical: `splits` went from a raw
passthrough to a field-by-field mapper, so four collections now have mappers — payments, requests,
splits, idempotency — and a fifth arrives at W10.

**I checked rather than raised it as a question.** The stored split in `splits.js` carries exactly `id`,
`callerId`, `amount`, `note`, `shares`, `requestIds`, `createdAt`, `sequence`; the mapper emits all
eight. Nothing is dropped. So there is no finding here and W8 should not be rejected for it — I am
telling you what I checked so you can disagree with the check rather than repeat it.

**Directed into W9 as criterion 13**, because W9 is where a dropped field stops being cosmetic and
becomes a lost account: the guard passes, the export is incomplete, the import restores less than it
received, and R10.11 is violated with nothing failing. The mechanism is the same derivation one level
down — enumerate `Object.keys()` of a live record, fail if a key is neither emitted nor on a commented
exclusion list naming what rebuilds it, demonstrated failing on a mapper with one field removed. Cheap,
because it is D30's shape and D44's rule applied one level in.

If you think it belongs at W8 after all, say so in the verdict and I will route it — the placement is my
call but the reasoning should survive contact with yours.

## Why criterion 13 is worded the way it is — the verifier saved it before it shipped

It built the naive version of that guard and ran it: it flagged `idempotency` as dropping
`bodyCanonical` and `responseBody`. Those are not dropped, they are **renamed** — `bodyCanonical → body`
(parsed, content preserved) and `responseBody → response`. **A key-name derivation at record level
cannot distinguish dropped from renamed, and four of your five mappers rename at least one field.** So
the naive guard fires on correct code: D51's failure mode inside the very mechanism built to prevent
D30's.

Hence the mapping list, and hence **both** demonstrations. A guard shown only to fire has not been shown
not to — that is D59 applied at write time rather than after the fact.

settlement is possible before W10 creates one.** So that half is carried to **W10 criterion 14**: export
a state containing a committed settlement, import it, confirm every member still carries its
`settlement_id`, the batch still resolves to its members, and a non-member still exposes
`settlement_id: null`. Do not build toward it here. Fifth instance of the pattern that produced D29,
D48, D52 and D54 — and this one was in my own reference list.

The verifier exercised the two-container harness before W9 is built, and it prevented a dilemma that would have landed on me.

**D62 — an instrument is exercised against real state before the item whose verdict depends on it, and a tolerance is demonstrated in both directions.**

Group 10's setup seeded "everything worth preserving," which quietly made every check in the group depend on *the last surface to exist* — settlements, W10. The R10.6 two-container check, mandatory for W9, died at `setup settlement` on a 404, one item early. At the W9 verdict my options would have been to reject conforming work for failing a check that needs W10, or accept W9 with the two-container path unexercised — and **the plan forbids the second**. So I'd have been choosing between an unjust rejection and a rule I wrote. It removed the choice a whole item before it arrived.

The fix is `status === 404 ? null : res`, tolerant of absence and strict about presence, with **both** halves demonstrated: route genuinely absent, the check proceeds and fails on `POST /_test/import` — W9's surface, the correct dependency; route present but broken behind a proxy answering 403, it hard-fails at setup as before. **"A tolerance shown only to tolerate has not been shown to stay strict"** is in the log verbatim — without the second demonstration the fix would be indistinguishable from "skip settlement seeding always," which would have disarmed group 10 at W10 instead of W9.

The finding underneath the finding: **that machinery had never once been run in this project**, and W9 is the first item that cannot be verified without it. A harness that has never run is indistinguishable from one that cannot — D59 one level out, with the instrument being the verification environment rather than a check.

**The wiring is now falsifiable**, and it's in criterion 2: `168 / 45 / 4` two-container against `168 / 44 / 5` single. A blocking count that does *not* rise by one means `ALT_BASE_URL` never reached the runner…

@[[cf49020e-4b68-450b-bca6-6da986b251ff]] Recorded as **D62**, and it prevented a dilemma that would have landed on me rather than on you. Suite at `f84e85f`. Plan rev 30 is published.

**Name the thing you avoided, because it is worth more than the fix.** Group 10's setup seeding "everything worth preserving" made every check in the group depend on *the last surface to exist*, so the mandatory R10.6 two-container check would have died at `setup settlement` on a 404 — one item early. At the W9 verdict my options would have been to reject conforming work for failing a check that needs W10, or to accept W9 with the two-container path unexercised. **The plan forbids the second**, so I would have been choosing between an unjust rejection and a rule I wrote. You removed the choice a whole item before it arrived.

**"A tolerance shown only to tolerate has not been shown to stay strict"** is the sharpest sentence in this family and it is in the log verbatim. `status === 404 ? null : res` is tolerant of absence and strict about presence, and the 403-behind-a-proxy demonstration is what establishes the second half — without it the fix would be indistinguishable from "skip the settlement seeding always", which would have silently disarmed group 10 at W10 instead of W9.

**That the harness had never run is the finding underneath the finding.** No container pair had been started in this project, and W9 is the first item that cannot be verified without one. A harness that has never run being indistinguishable from one that cannot is D59 one level out again — and this time the instrument was the *verification environment* rather than a check. D62 now says an instrument gets exercised against real state before the item whose verdict depends on it.

**The falsifiable wiring signal is in criterion 2 now**: `168 / 45 / 4` two-container against `168 / 44 / 5` single, and a blocking count that does not rise by one means `ALT_BASE_URL` never reached the runner. A test setup you can tell is *actually connected* is rarer than it should be, and it removes the failure mode where the two-container path silently degrades to a single-container pass. Worth saying that the count going **up** being the good sign is counterintuitive enough that stating it was necessary.

**On the three corrections** — I take your reframe and it is fairer than mine, but I am keeping my version in the log alongside it. The gap between a property and an instrument is real and structural, and criterion 13's rename problem genuinely was only findable by building the naive guard and watching it misfire. What I want the record to keep is that all three were found by *you* rather than by me, and the fix in each case was available cheaply at write time. A coordinator who writes a property and does not ask what would measure it is producing criteria that read well and cannot be run — that diagnosis is useful to me even if the error is structural rather than careless.

One correction of my own in the same vein: criterion 2's `ALT_BASE_URL` clause was in my assignment message to the implementer and **not in the plan**, which is the D38 failure I wrote D38 to stop. Fixed in rev 30, with the wiring signal added to the same criterion.

Suite head **`e3f9ad0`**. Not a W9 matter — this lands on **R2.5 and W11** — but it is a documentation defect in my own instrument and it was about to become evidence.

**I applied D62 to itself.** The rule says an instrument gets exercised against real state before the item whose verdict depends on it. My README and COVERAGE.md have claimed since A0 that the suite "runs unchanged against a container started with `--network none`", and nobody had tried it. W11 verifies R2.5, so that sentence was queued to be cited as proof.

**It is false as written.** `--network none` removes every interface, so a published port is inert and the suite cannot reach the service from the host — `curl` gets no answer at all. COVERAGE.md went further and said the suite "is designed to pass in exactly that configuration, which is how it contributes evidence." In that configuration it could not connect, let alone pass. A gap reason that names a method nobody has run is the same class as a guard that has never fired.

**The substance holds, and is stronger than what was claimed.** Mount the suite read-only and run it *inside* the container against loopback:

    docker run -d --name iso --network none -e PORT=8080 \
      -v "$(pwd)/stage-1/acceptance:/suite:ro" <image>
    docker exec -e BASE_URL=http://127.0.0.1:8080 iso node /suite/main.mjs

Container has only `lo`, outbound confirmed blocked, DNS unavailable — and the suite returns **168 / 44 / 5, identical to the host-side run at the same commit**. That is a demonstration of R2.5 rather than an assertion about one, and it is a stricter configuration than the original claim described: not "no outbound route" but "no interfaces whatsoever".

Also tried and rejected: an `--internal` docker network blocks inbound too, so the host still cannot reach the service. Worth recording so W11 does not spend the attempt.

Corrected in `README.md`, `lib/inventory.mjs` (R2.5's gap reason) and the generated `COVERAGE.md` — and I then re-ran the written procedure verbatim, because instructions that have not been followed as printed are the same problem one level down. They work as printed.

**For W11:** R2.5's evidence is now a command anyone can run, with an expected number attached. The three out-of-band gaps in COVERAGE.md — R2.5, R2.7 and R10.17 — are the remaining places where a reason stands in for a check, and R2.5 was the one whose reason did not work. I will check the other two before W11 rather than at it.

D62 says an instrument gets exercised before the item whose verdict depends on it. I applied that rule to itself and found a documentation defect in my own instrument that was about to become evidence.

My README and `COVERAGE.md` have claimed since A0 that the suite "runs unchanged against a container started with `--network none`". Nobody had tried it, and W11 verifies R2.5, so that sentence was queued to be cited as proof.

**It's false as written.** `--network none` removes every interface, so a published port is inert and the suite can't reach the service from the host — curl gets no answer. `COVERAGE.md` went further: the suite "is designed to pass in exactly that configuration, which is how it contributes evidence." In that configuration it couldn't connect, let alone pass. A gap reason naming a method nobody has run is the same class as a guard that has never fired.

The substance holds and is *stronger* than the claim: mount the suite read-only and run it inside the container against loopback. Only `lo`, outbound confirmed blocked, DNS unavailable — and the suite returns `168 / 44 / 5`, identical to the host-side run at the same commit. That's a demonstration rather than an assertion, and a stricter configuration than originally described: not "no outbound route" but "no interfaces whatsoever". I also tried an `--internal` network and rejected it — it blocks inbound too, so W11 needn't spend the attempt.

Then I re-ran the corrected procedure verbatim, because instructions that haven't been followed as printed are the same problem one level down.

The thing I'll carry forward: R2.5 was one of three references where `COVERAGE.md` has a *reason* standing in for a check, and its reason didn't work. The other two are R2.7 and R10.17. I've tracked checking those before W11 rather than at it — a reason that has never been executed is indistinguishable from one that can't be.
